 PAGASA broke ground on a Bataan radar meant to catch the storms bigger forecasts miss
 PAGASA and Bataan Peninsula State University broke ground on 27 October 2026 for an S-band Doppler radar in Abucay, built to read rainfall, wind speed and storm tracks over Bataan and western Luzon, with a research role for university students. #PAGASA #DopplerRadar #Bataan #WeatherForecasting #Philippines
 by 
 ASTIG PR 
 4 hours ago 4 hours ago 
 Advertisements 
 PAGASA broke ground on 27 October 2026 for a weather radar station in Abucay, Bataan, built to watch the kind of fast-forming storms that flood a handful of towns before a national forecast has caught up with them.
 The facility, on the Abucay campus of Bataan Peninsula State University, will house an S-band magnetron-type Doppler weather radar. PAGASA says it is meant to track convective storms and small rainbands that broader forecasts can miss, and to deliver real-time readings on rainfall volume, wind velocity and storm tracks for Bataan and western Luzon.
 Work on the radar tower is now under way. The agency has not announced a date for switching the station on.
 What an S-band radar does
 Doppler radars send out radio pulses and read the returning signal to work out how much water is falling, and which way the wind carrying it is moving. Longer-wavelength S-band sets like this one are the standard choice for tropical settings because heavy rain is less likely to drown out the signal returning to the dish.
 PAGASA expects the Abucay station to close a local monitoring gap, giving forecasters a finer look at rainbands that develop over one municipality and move on within hours.
 That territory includes Bataan’s own towns and the coastline facing the South China Sea, as well as the approach to Manila Bay.
 Warnings that talk about impact, not just rain
 DOST Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. tied the project to impact-based forecasting, in which a warning tells local governments what a storm will do to farms, homes and roads rather than only how much rain is expected.
 “Protecting lives will always be our highest priority. But true resilience means protecting livelihoods as well,” Solidum said at the ceremony, naming the crops farmers grow, the small businesses that sustain families and the infrastructure a community needs after a storm. 
 Better information, he said, gives local leaders and families the power to take preventive action and minimize losses before disaster strikes. PAGASA Administrator Nathaniel Servando said the Abucay station would improve forecasts and warnings, and let emergency managers and communities act earlier.
 Why put a radar on a university campus
 The Abucay site is not just an observation post. Once the station is running, PAGASA says it will serve as a research asset for BPSU engineering and environmental science students, with direct access to real-time radar data streams.
 The partnership that put it there is older than the groundbreaking. PAGASA and the university signed a memorandum of agreement in September 2025 to build the radar station on the Abucay campus.
 Abucay sits on the eastern shore of Bataan, roughly across Manila Bay from the capital and well within the track that southwest monsoon rainbands and habagat-enhanced storms follow in a normal year.
 A network stretched by this month’s weather
 The groundbreaking lands in a demanding week for the weather bureau. Also on 27 October, PAGASA declared the onset of the northeast monsoon season while warning that a very strong El Niño is still building, a combination that puts drought and heat alongside the cooler months.
 The country’s warning systems have also been in the spotlight this month, after an international risk poll found four in five Filipino adults had been hit by a disaster in five years, the highest share among the 140 countries surveyed.
 Key facts on the Abucay radar

 ASTIG.PH has followed the country’s weather year closely, including the amihan declaration and its La Niña flood warning and Typhoon Rosal’s exit, which shut Basco Airport .
